summary: Defines a metric for one-way packet loss across Internet paths. It builds on the IPPM framework in RFC 2330 and makes RFC 2680 obsolete.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7680 defines how to measure packet loss in one direction between two hosts. It specifies how to score one packet, how to select a sample of packets and how to report the resulting loss ratio.

subtitle: A standard metric for whether IP packets arrive in one direction across a path.

tldr.problem: Round-trip measurements combine forward and reverse paths, so they can hide which direction loses packets. Measurements need a consistent definition for one-way loss.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines one packet's loss value as 0 when received and 1 when not received within Tmax. It then defines Poisson-timed samples and statistics such as the average loss ratio.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7680 is Internet Standard STD 82 and obsoletes RFC 2680, defining common measurement terms and reporting requirements.

today: RFC 7680 is an Internet Standard (STD 82) that obsoletes RFC 2680. The unit metadata lists no RFC that updates or obsoletes it.

sections.title: A Metric in Three Steps
sections.content:
RFC 7680 defines one-way packet loss across Internet paths and builds on the IP Performance Metrics framework. It organizes the measurement into a singleton for one packet, a sample containing many singleton results, and statistics calculated from that sample.

The singleton metric records one packet's outcome. The sample uses times selected from a Poisson process. A statistic such as a loss ratio then summarizes the sample. Keeping these levels separate helps make measurements comparable.
sections.plainLanguage: The metric first scores one packet, then collects many scores, then calculates a summary. This separation makes it clear what each result describes.

sections.title: Why Measure Each Direction
sections.content:
Some applications perform poorly when packet loss is high, and excessive loss can make real-time communication difficult. Loss can also make it harder for transport protocols to sustain high bandwidth.

A round trip may use different forward and reverse paths, and even symmetric paths can have different queuing behavior in each direction. Applications may rely more on one direction, and quality-of-service settings may differ by direction. Measuring each direction separately can identify these differences.

The RFC defines measurement metrics; it does not specify exactly how each application should use them.
sections.plainLanguage: A packet may travel one route while the reply uses another. Measuring each direction separately shows where loss occurs instead of combining both paths into one result.

sections.title: The Single-Packet Loss Value
sections.content:
The singleton uses source address Src, destination address Dst, send time T and loss threshold Tmax. Its value is 0 if the destination receives the Type-P packet and 1 if the packet is not received within Tmax.

A corrupted packet counts as lost. If multiple non-corrupt copies arrive, the packet counts as received. A fragmented packet that is not reassembled counts as lost. The metric corresponds to one-way delay: loss is 0 when delay is finite and 1 when delay is undefined.

Times are measured in seconds relative to UTC. Clock synchronization, accuracy, resolution and skew affect the interpretation of measurements.
sections.plainLanguage: A packet receives a value of 0 if it arrives and 1 if it does not arrive within the chosen waiting time. A corrupted packet or an unreassembled fragment counts as lost.

sections.title: Measuring and Reporting Loss
sections.content:
A general method synchronizes clocks at Src and Dst, sends a selected Type-P test packet with a timestamp, and checks whether it arrives before Tmax. The RFC leaves the packet format and clock-coordination method outside its scope.

Errors can result from clock synchronization, a poorly chosen loss threshold or resource limits on the receiving measurement instrument. A threshold that is too low can count delivered packets as lost, and an overloaded receiver can drop a packet after the network has delivered it.

Reports must state the Type-P used, Tmax and the degree of clock synchronization. They should also report the path when possible. The instrument should be calibrated to reduce the chance that local resource limits are mistaken for network loss.
sections.plainLanguage: Measurements need clocks that agree and a stated waiting time for packets. Reports must include the packet type and threshold so readers can interpret the result.

sections.title: Samples at Poisson Times
sections.content:
A sample fixes Src, Dst and Type-P, then selects packet send times between T0 and Tf using a pseudorandom Poisson process with average rate lambda. The sample is a sequence of time-and-loss pairs and is empty if no packets were measured.

Poisson sampling helps reduce bias and self-synchronization effects. A rate that is too high can add traffic and cause congestion; a rate that is too low may miss network behavior. Other sampling approaches, including truncated Poisson and periodic sampling with random start times, may suit different situations.

Measurements must account for test packets arriving out of order. The RFC points to separate IPPM work for packet reordering metrics.
sections.plainLanguage: The sample sends test packets at randomized times rather than on a fixed schedule. Sending too many can affect the network, while sending too few can miss changes.

sections.title: Calculating the Loss Ratio
sections.content:
The Type-P-One-way-Packet-Loss-Ratio is the average of the sample's 0 and 1 values, or the number of losses divided by the number of packets. The ratio is undefined for an empty sample.

In the RFC's example, one of five packets is lost, so the ratio is 0.2. The RFC notes that distinguishing small loss rates may require many samples, and measurement-instrument drops can make a low loss ratio meaningless if they are not negligible compared with the loss being measured.
sections.plainLanguage: The loss ratio is the share of sampled packets that were lost. If one of five packets is lost, the ratio is 0.2.

sections.title: Security and Privacy of Measurements
sections.content:
Active measurements add packets to the network, so their parameters must keep that traffic trivial. Too much measurement traffic can distort results and, in extreme cases, contribute to congestion or denial of service.

Measurements can also be manipulated if routers treat test traffic differently from normal traffic or if an attacker injects accepted test packets. Measurement methods should make test traffic difficult to distinguish from normal traffic, and authentication such as digital signatures may help guard against injection.

Access to measurement results and control of measurement systems should be protected against reconnaissance. The RFC notes that passive measurement of user traffic raises additional privacy issues.
sections.plainLanguage: Test traffic must be small enough not to disrupt the network. Measurement systems should also guard against fake test packets and protect results from misuse.
